senses.d: A Hebrew patriarch (son of Isaac, and ancestor of the Jews), who in a vision saw a ladder reaching up to heaven (Gen. xxviii. 12); — also called Israel.
q: And Jacob said . . . with my staff I passed over this Jordan, and now I am become two bands.
Thy name shall be called no more Jacob, but Israel.

senses.d: Jehovah.
A kind of frock for children.
To press into a close or tight position; to crowd; to squeeze; to wedge in.
q: The ship . . . jammed in between two rocks.

senses.d: To crush or bruise; as, to jam a finger in the crack of a door.
To bring (a vessel) so close to the wind that half her upper sails are laid aback.

Jam.etym: [Either fr. jamb, as if squeezed between jambs, or more likely from the same source as champ See Champ.]

senses.d: A mass of people or objects crowded together; also, the pressure from a crowd; a crush; as, a jam in a street; a jam of logs in a river.
An injury caused by jamming.
A preserve of fruit boiled with sugar and water; as, raspberry jam; currant jam; grape jam.

Jam.etym: [Prob. fr. jam, v.; but cf. also Ar. jamad ice, jelly, jāmid congealed, jamd congelation, ice.]

senses.d: One of an intermediate order between angels and men.
To sound harshly or discordantly, as bells out of tune.
To talk idly; to prate; to babble; to chatter; to gossip.
To quarrel in words; to altercate; to wrangle.
q: Good wits will be jangling; but, gentles, agree.
Prussian Trenck . . . jargons and jangles in an unmelodious manner.

Jangle.etym: [OE. janglen to quarrel, OF. jangler to rail, quarrel; of Dutch or German origin; cf. D. jangelen, janken, to whimper, chide, brawl, quarrel.]

senses.d: To cause to sound harshly or inharmoniously; to produce discordant sounds with.
q: Like sweet bells jangled, out of tune, and harsh.

senses.d: Idle talk; prate; chatter; babble.
Discordant sound; wrangling.
q: The musical jangle of sleigh bells.

senses.d: Producing discordant sounds.
Idle babbling; vain disputation.
q: From which some, having swerved, have turned aside unto vain jangling.

senses.d: Wrangling; altercation.
A turn.
A deep, broad-mouthed vessel of earthenware or glass, for holding fruit, preserves, etc., or for ornamental purposes; as, a jar of honey; a rose jar.
The measure of what is contained in a jar; as, a jar of oil; a jar of preserves.

Jar.etym: [F. jarre, Sp. jarra, from Ar. jarrah ewer; cf. Pers. jarrah.]

senses.d: To give forth a rudely quivering or tremulous sound; to sound harshly or discordantly; as, the notes jarred on my ears.
q: When such strings jar, what hope of harmony ?
A string may jar in the best master's hand.

senses.d: To act in opposition or disagreement; to clash; to interfere; to quarrel; to dispute.
q: When those renowned noble peers Greece Through stubborn pride among themselves did jar.
For orders and degrees Jar not with liberty, but well consist.

Jar.etym: [Cf. OE. charken to creak, AS. cearcian to gnash, F. jars a gander, L. garrire to chatter, prate, OHG. kerran to chatter, croak, G. quarren to grumble, and E. jargon, ajar.]

senses.d: To cause a short, tremulous motion of, to cause to tremble, as by a sudden shock or blow; to shake; to shock; as, to jar the earth; to jar one's faith.
To tick; to beat; to mark or tell off.
q: My thoughts are minutes, and with sighs they jar Their watches on unto mine eyes.

senses.d: A rattling, tremulous vibration or shock; a shake; a harsh sound; a discord; as, the jar of a train; the jar of harsh sounds.
Clash of interest or opinions; collision; discord; debate; slight disagreement.
q: And yet his peace is but continual jar.
Cease, cease these jars, and rest your minds in peace.

senses.d: A regular vibration, as of a pendulum.
q: I love thee not a jar of the clock.

senses.d: In deep well boring, a device resembling two long chain links, for connecting a percussion drill to the rod or rope which works it, so that the drill is driven down by impact and is jerked loose when jammed.
Jasper.

An opaque, impure variety of quartz, of red, yellow, and other dull colors, breaking with a smooth surface. It admits of a high polish, and is used for vases, seals, snuff boxes, etc. When the colors are in stripes or bands, it is called striped or banded jasper. The Egyptian pebble is a brownish yellow jasper.

Jasper.etym: [OE. jaspre, jaspe, OF. jaspre, jaspe, F. jaspe, L. iaspis, Gr. �; cf. Per. yashp, yashf, Ar. yashb, yasb, yasf, Heb. yāshpheh. Cf. Diaper.]

senses.d: A sort of light spear, to be thrown or cast by the hand; anciently, a weapon of war used by horsemen and foot soldiers; now used chiefly in hunting the wild boar and other fierce game.
q: Flies the javelin swifter to its mark, Launched by the vigor of a Roman arm?

Javelin.etym: [F. javeline; akin to Sp. jabalina, It. giavelina, and F. javelot, OF. gavlot. Cf. Gavelock.]

senses.d: To pierce with a javelin.
One of the bones, usually bearing teeth, which form the framework of the mouth.
Fig.: Anything resembling the jaw of an animal in form or action; esp., pl., the mouth or way of entrance; as, the jaws of a pass; the jaws of darkness; the jaws of death.
A notch or opening.
The inner end of a boom or gaff, hollowed in a half circle so as to move freely on a mast.
Impudent or abusive talk.

Jaw.etym: [A modification of chaw, formed under the influence of F. joue the cheek. See Chaw, Chew.]

senses.d: To scold; to clamor.
To assail or abuse by scolding.
The bone of either jaw; a maxilla or a mandible.
Zealous; solicitous; vigilant; anxiously watchful.
q: I have been very jealous for the Lord God of hosts.
How nicely jealous is every one of us of his own repute!

senses.d: Apprehensive; anxious; suspiciously watchful.
q: 'This doing wrong creates such doubts as these, Renders us jealous and disturbs our peace.
The people are so jealous of the clergy's ambition.

senses.d: Exacting exclusive devotion; intolerant of rivalry.
q: Thou shalt worship no other God; for the Lord, whose name is Jealous, is a jealous God.

senses.d: Disposed to suspect rivalry in matters of interest and affection; apprehensive regarding the motives of possible rivals, or the fidelity of friends; distrustful; having morbid fear of rivalry in love or preference given to another; painfully suspicious of the faithfulness of husband, wife, or lover.
q: If the spirit of jealousy come upon him, and he be jealous of his wife.
To both these sisters have I sworn my love: Each jealous of the other, as the stung Are of the adder.
It is one of the best bonds, both of chastity and obedience, in the wife, if she think her husband wise; which she will never do if she find him jealous.

Jealous.etym: [OE. jalous, gelus, OF. jalous, F. jaloux, LL. zelosus zealous, fr. zelus emulation, zeal, jealousy, Gr. ζη̑λοσ. See Zeal, and cf. Zealous.]

senses.d: The quality of being jealous; earnest concern or solicitude; painful apprehension of rivalship in cases nearly affecting one's happiness; painful suspicion of the faithfulness of husband, wife, or lover.
q: I was jealous for jealousy.
Jealousy is the . . . apprehension of superiority.
Whoever had qualities to alarm our jealousy, had excellence to deserve our fondness.

Jealousy.etym: [ F. jalousie. See Jealous, and cf. Jalousie.]

senses.d: A Scripture name of the Supreme Being, by which he was revealed to the Jews as their covenant God or Sovereign of the theocracy; the “ineffable name” of the Supreme Being, which was not pronounced by the Jews.

Jehovah.etym: [Heb. usually yĕhōvāh (with the vowel points of ădōnāi Lord), sometimes (to avoid repetition) yĕhōvih (with the vowel points of ĕlōhīm God); but only the four Heb, consonants yhvh are conceded to be certainly known.]

senses.d: A coachman; a driver; especially, one who drives furiously.

Jehu.etym: [From Jehu, son of Nimshi. 2 Kings ix. 20.]

senses.d: To put in jeopardy; to expose to loss or injury; to imperil; to hazard.
q: A people that jeoparded their lives unto the death.

Jeopard.syn: To hazard; risk; imperil; endanger; expose.

senses.d: Exposure to death, loss, or injury; hazard; danger.
q: There came down a storm of wind on the lake; and they were filled with water, and were in jeopardy.
Look to thyself, thou art in jeopardy.

Jeopardy.syn: Danger; peril; hazard; risk. See Danger.
Jeopardy.etym: [OE. jupartie, juperti, jeuparti, OF. jeu parti an even game, a game in which the chances are even; OF. jeu, ju, F. jeu (L. jocus jest) + F. partier to divide, L. partire to divide. See Joke, and Part.]

senses.d: To jeopardize.
The chief city of Palestine, intimately associated with the glory of the Jewish nation, and the life and death of Jesus Christ.
Any representation or suggestion of the genealogy of Christ, in decorative art
A genealogical tree represented in stained glass.
A candlestick with many branches, each of which bears the name of some one of the descendants of Jesse; — called also tree of Jesse.

Jesse.etym: [LL. Jesse, the father of David, fr. Gr. �, fr. Herb. Yishai.]

senses.d: A deed; an action; a gest.
q: The jests or actions of princes.

senses.d: A mask; a pageant; an interlude.
q: He promised us, in honor of our guest, To grace our banquet with some pompous jest.

senses.d: Something done or said in order to amuse; a joke; a witticism; a jocose or sportive remark or phrase. See Synonyms under Jest, v. i.
q: I must be sad . . . smile at no man's jests.
The Right Honorable gentleman is indebted to his memory for his jests, and to his imagination for his facts.

senses.d: The object of laughter or sport; a laughingstock.
q: Then let me be your jest; I deserve it.

Jest.etym: [OE. jeste, geste, deed, action, story, tale, OF. geste, LL. gesta, orig., exploits, neut. pl. from L. gestus, p. p. of gerere to bear, carry, accomplish, perform; perh. orig., to make to come, bring, and perh. akin to E. come. Cf. Gest a deed, Register, n.]

senses.d: To take part in a merrymaking; — especially, to act in a mask or interlude.
To make merriment by words or actions; to joke; to make light of anything.
q: He jests at scars that never felt a wound.

senses.d: Sportive; not serious; fit for jests.
q: He will find that these are no jesting matters.

senses.d: The act or practice of making jests; joking; pleasantry.
One of a religious order founded by Ignatius Loyola, and approved in 1540, under the title of The Society of Jesus.
Fig.: A crafty person; an intriguer.

Jesuit.etym: [F. Jésuite, Sp. Jesuita: cf. It. Gesuita.]

senses.d: The Savior; the name of the Son of God as announced by the angel to his parents; the personal name of Our Lord, in distinction from Christ, his official appellation.
q: Thou shalt call his name Jesus; for he shall save his people from their sins.
Jesu, do thou my soul receive.

Jesus.etym: [L. Jesus, Gr. �, from Heb. Yēshūa'; Yāh Jehovah + hōshīa' to help.]

senses.d: Originally, one belonging to the tribe or kingdom of Judah; after the return from the Babylonish captivity, any member of the new state; a Hebrew; an Israelite.

Jew.etym: [OF. Juis, pl., F. Juif, L. Judaeus, Gr. �, fr. � the country of the Jews, Judea, fr. Heb. Y�h�dāh Judah, son of Jacob. Cf. Judaic.]

senses.d: An ornament of dress usually made of a precious metal, and having enamel or precious stones as a part of its design.
q: Plate of rare device, and jewels Of rich and exquisite form.

senses.d: A precious stone; a gem.
An object regarded with special affection; a precious thing.
A bearing for a pivot a pivot in a watch, formed of a crystal or precious stone, as a ruby.

Jewel.etym: [OE. juel, jowel, OF. jouel, juel, joiel, F. joyau, dim. of OF. joie joy, jewel, F. joie joy. See Joy.]

senses.d: To dress, adorn, deck, or supply with jewels, as a dress, a sword hilt, or a watch; to bespangle, as with jewels.
q: The long gray tufts . . . are jeweled thick with dew.

senses.d: A Hebrew woman.
Of or pertaining to the Jews or Hebrews; characteristic of or resembling the Jews or their customs; Israelitish.
Judea; also, a district inhabited by Jews; a Jews' quarter.
q: Teaching throughout all Jewry.

senses.d: A bold, vicious woman; a termagant.

Jezebel.etym: [From Jezebel, Heb. Izebel, the wife of Ahab king of Israel.]

senses.d: A sweetheart; a darling.
A sudden thrust or stab; a jab.
A piece of chance or occasional work; any definite work undertaken in gross for a fixed price; as, he did the job for a thousand dollars.
A public transaction done for private profit; something performed ostensibly as a part of official duty, but really for private gain; a corrupt official business.
Any affair or event which affects one, whether fortunately or unfortunately.
A situation or opportunity of work; as, he lost his job.

Job.etym: [Prov. E. job, gob, n., a small piece of wood, v., to stab, strike; cf. E. gob, gobbet; perh. influenced by E. chop to cut off, to mince. See Gob.]

senses.d: To strike or stab with a pointed instrument.
To thrust in, as a pointed instrument.
To do or cause to be done by separate portions or lots; to sublet (work); as, to job a contract.
To buy and sell, as a broker; to purchase of importers or manufacturers for the purpose of selling to retailers; as, to job goods.
To hire or let by the job or for a period of service; as, to job a carriage.
To do chance work for hire; to work by the piece; to do petty work.
q: Authors of all work, to job for the season.

senses.d: To seek private gain under pretense of public service; to turn public matters to private advantage.
q: And judges job, and bishops bite the town.

senses.d: To carry on the business of a jobber in merchandise or stocks.
The hero of the book of that name in the Old Testament; the typical patient man.
A proper name of a man.
To bring together, literally or figuratively; to place in contact; to connect; to couple; to unite; to combine; to associate; to add; to append.
q: Woe unto them that join house to house.
Held up his left hand, which did flame and burn Like twenty torches joined.
Thy tuneful voice with numbers join.

senses.d: To associate one's self to; to be or become connected with; to league one's self with; to unite with; as, to join a party; to join the church.
q: We jointly now to join no other head.

senses.d: To unite in marriage.
q: He that joineth his virgin in matrimony.
What, therefore, God hath joined together, let not man put asunder.

senses.d: To enjoin upon; to command.
q: They join them penance, as they call it.

senses.d: To accept, or engage in, as a contest; as, to join encounter, battle, issue.

Join.syn: To add; annex; unite; connect; combine; consociate; couple; link; append. See Add.
Join.etym: [OE. joinen, joignen, F. joindre, fr. L. jungere to yoke, bind together, join; akin to jugum yoke. See Yoke, and cf. Conjugal, Junction, Junta.]

senses.d: To be contiguous, close, or in contact; to come together; to unite; to mingle; to form a union; as, the bones of the skull join; two rivers join.
q: Whose house joined hard to the synagogue.
Should we again break thy commandments, and join in affinity with the people of these abominations?
Nature and fortune joined to make thee great.

senses.d: The line joining two points; the point common to two intersecting lines.

The place or part where two things or parts are joined or united; the union of two or more smooth or even surfaces admitting of a close-fitting or junction; junction; as, a joint between two pieces of timber; a joint in a pipe.
A joining of two things or parts so as to admit of motion; an articulation, whether movable or not; a hinge; as, the knee joint; a node or joint of a stem; a ball and socket joint. See Articulation.
q: A scaly gauntlet now, with joints of steel, Must glove this hand.
To tear thee joint by joint.

senses.d: The part or space included between two joints, knots, nodes, or articulations; as, a joint of cane or of a grass stem; a joint of the leg.
Any one of the large pieces of meat, as cut into portions by the butcher for roasting.
A plane of fracture, or divisional plane, of a rock transverse to the stratification.
The space between the adjacent surfaces of two bodies joined and held together, as by means of cement, mortar, etc.; as, a thin joint.
The means whereby the meeting surfaces of pieces in a structure are secured together.

Joint.etym: [F. joint, fr. joindre, p. p. joint. See Join.]

senses.d: Joined; united; combined; concerted; as, joint action.
Involving the united activity of two or more; done or produced by two or more working together.
q: I read this joint effusion twice over.

senses.d: United, joined, or sharing with another or with others; not solitary in interest or action; holding in common with an associate, or with associates; acting together; as, joint heir; joint creditor; joint debtor, etc.
Shared by, or affecting two or more; held in common; as, joint property; a joint bond.
q: A joint burden laid upon us all.

Joint.etym: [F., p. p. of joindre. See Join.]

senses.d: To unite by a joint or joints; to fit together; to prepare so as to fit together; as, to joint boards.
q: Pierced through the yielding planks of jointed wood.

senses.d: To join; to connect; to unite; to combine.
q: Jointing their force 'gainst Cæsar.

senses.d: To provide with a joint or joints; to articulate.
q: The fingers are jointed together for motion.

senses.d: To separate the joints; of; to divide at the joint or joints; to disjoint; to cut up into joints, as meat.
q: Quartering, jointing, seething, and roasting.

senses.d: To fit as if by joints; to coalesce as joints do; as, the stones joint, neatly.
A projecting or retreating part in something; any irregularity of line or surface, as in a wall.
A narrow piece of scenery used to join together two flats or wings of an interior setting.
A place of low resort, as for smoking opium.
The Hebrew prophet, who was cast overboard as one who endangered the ship; hence, any person whose presence is unpropitious.
A pot or vessel with a large neck, formerly used by physicians and alchemists.
A chamber pot.

Jordan.etym: [Prob. fr. the river Jordan, and shortened fr. Jordan bottle a bottle of water from the Jordan, brought back by pilgrims.]

senses.d: An outer garment worn in the 18th century; esp., a woman's riding habit, buttoned down the front.
An iota; a point; a tittle; the smallest particle. Cf. Bit, n.
q: Till heaven and earth pass, one jot or one tittle shall in no wise pass from the law, till all be fulfilled.
Neither will they bate One jot of ceremony.

Jot.etym: [L. iota, Gr. � the name of the letter (E. i, Heb. y�d), the smallest letter of the Greek alphabet. Cf. Iota.]

senses.d: To set down; to make a brief note of; — usually followed by down.
The travel or work of a day.
q: We have yet large day, for scarce the sun Hath finished half his journey.

senses.d: Travel or passage from one place to another; hence, figuratively, a passage through life.
q: The good man . . . is gone a long journey.
We must all have the same journey's end.

Journey.etym: [OE. jornee, journee, prop., a day's journey, OF. jornée, jurnée, a day, a day's work of journey, F. journée, fr. OF. jorn, jurn, jor a day, F. jour, fr. L. diurnus. See Journal.]

senses.d: To travel from place to place; to go from home to a distance.
q: Abram journeyed, going on still toward the south.

senses.d: To traverse; to travel over or through.

The passion or emotion excited by the acquisition or expectation of good; pleasurable feelings or emotions caused by success, good fortune, and the like, or by a rational prospect of possessing what we love or desire; gladness; exhilaration of spirits; delight.
q: Her heavenly form beheld, all wished her joy.
Glides the smooth current of domestic joy.
Who, for the joy that was set before him, endured the cross, despising the shame.
Tears of true joy for his return.
Joy is a delight of the mind, from the consideration of the present or assured approaching possession of a good.

senses.d: That which causes joy or happiness.
q: For ye are our glory and joy.
A thing of beauty is a joy forever.

senses.d: The sign or exhibition of joy; gayety; mirth; merriment; festivity.
q: Such joy made Una, when her knight she found.
The roofs with joy resound.

Joy.syn: Gladness; pleasure; delight; happiness; exultation; transport; felicity; ecstasy; rapture; bliss; gayety; mirth; merriment; festivity; hilarity.
Joy.etym: [OE. joye, OF. joye, joie, goie, F. joie, L. gaudia, pl. of gaudium joy, fr. gaudere to rejoice, to be glad; cf. Gr. � to rejoice, � proud. Cf. Gaud, Jewel.]

senses.d: To rejoice; to be glad; to delight; to exult.
q: I will joy in the God of my salvation.
In whose sight all things joy.

Joy.etym: [OF. joir, F. jouir. See Joy, n.]

senses.d: To give joy to; to congratulate.
q: To joy the friend, or grapple with the foe.

senses.d: To gladden; to make joyful; to exhilarate.
q: Neither pleasure's art can joy my spirits.

senses.d: To enjoy.
q: Who might have lived and joyed immortal bliss.

senses.d: Full of joy; having or causing joy; very glad; as, a joyful heart.
q: My soul shall be joyful in my God.
Sad for their loss, but joyful of our life.

senses.d: Glad; gay; merry; joyful; also, affording or inspiring joy; with of before the word or words expressing the cause of joy.
q: Is this your joyous city?
They all as glad as birds of joyous prime.
And joyous of our conquest early won.

Joyous.syn: Merry; lively; blithe; gleeful; gay; glad; mirthful; sportive; festive; joyful; happy; blissful; charming; delightful.
Joyous.etym: [OE. joyous, joious, joios, F. joyeux.See Joy.]

senses.d: The disciple who betrayed Christ. Hence: A treacherous person; one who betrays under the semblance of friendship.
Treacherous; betraying.
A public officer who is invested with authority to hear and determine litigated causes, and to administer justice between parties in courts held for that purpose.
q: The parts of a judge in hearing are four: to direct the evidence; to moderate length, repetition, or impertinency of speech; to recapitulate, select, and collate the material points of that which hath been said; and to give the rule or sentence.

senses.d: One who has skill, knowledge, or experience, sufficient to decide on the merits of a question, or on the quality or value of anything; one who discerns properties or relations with skill and readiness; a connoisseur; an expert; a critic.
q: A man who is no judge of law may be a good judge of poetry, or eloquence, or of the merits of a painting.

senses.d: A person appointed to decide in a trial of skill, speed, etc., between two or more parties; an umpire; as, a judge in a horse race.
One of the supreme magistrates, with both civil and military powers, who governed Israel for more than four hundred years.
The title of the seventh book of the Old Testament; the Book of Judges.

Judge.etym: [OE. juge, OF. & F. juge, fr. OF. jugier, F. juger, to judge. See Judge, v. i.]

senses.d: To hear and determine, as in causes on trial; to decide as a judge; to give judgment; to pass sentence.
q: The Lord judge between thee and me.
Father, who art judge Of all things made, and judgest only right!

senses.d: To assume the right to pass judgment on another; to sit in judgment or commendation; to criticise or pass adverse judgment upon others. See Judge, v. t., 3.
q: Forbear to judge, for we are sinners all.

senses.d: To compare facts or ideas, and perceive their relations and attributes, and thus distinguish truth from falsehood; to determine; to discern; to distinguish; to form an opinion about.
q: Judge not according to the appearance.
She is wise if I can judge of her.

Judge.etym: [OE. jugen, OF. jugier, F. juger, L. judicare, fr. judex judge; jus law or right + dicare to proclaim, pronounce, akin to dicere to say. See Just, a., and Diction, and cf. Judicial.]

senses.d: To hear and determine by authority, as a case before a court, or a controversy between two parties.
To examine and pass sentence on; to try; to doom.
q: God shall judge the righteous and the wicked.
To bring my whole cause 'fore his holiness, And to be judged by him.

senses.d: To arrogate judicial authority over; to sit in judgment upon; to be censorious toward.
q: Judge not, that ye be not judged.

senses.d: To determine upon or deliberation; to esteem; to think; to reckon.
q: If ye have judged me to be faithful to the Lord.

senses.d: To exercise the functions of a magistrate over; to govern.
q: Make us a king to judge us.

senses.d: The act of judging; the operation of the mind, involving comparison and discrimination, by which a knowledge of the values and relations of thins, whether of moral qualities, intellectual concepts, logical propositions, or material facts, is obtained; as, by careful judgment he avoided the peril; by a series of wrong judgments he forfeited confidence.
q: I oughte deme, of skilful jugement, That in the salte sea my wife is deed.

senses.d: The power or faculty of performing such operations (see 1); esp., when unqualified, the faculty of judging or deciding rightly, justly, or wisely; good sense; as, a man of judgment; a politician without judgment.
q: He shall judge thy people with righteousness and thy poor with judgment.
Hernia. I would my father look'd but with my eyes. Theseus. Rather your eyes must with his judgment look.

senses.d: The conclusion or result of judging; an opinion; a decision.
q: She in my judgment was as fair as you.
Who first his judgment asked, and then a place.

senses.d: The act of determining, as in courts of law, what is conformable to law and justice; also, the determination, decision, or sentence of a court, or of a judge; the mandate or sentence of God as the judge of all.
q: In judgments between rich and poor, consider not what the poor man needs, but what is his own.
Most heartily I do beseech the court To give the judgment.

senses.d: That act of the mind by which two notions or ideas which are apprehended as distinct are compared for the purpose of ascertaining their agreement or disagreement. See 1. The comparison may be threefold: (1) Of individual objects forming a concept. (2) Of concepts giving what is technically called a judgment. (3) Of two judgments giving an inference. Judgments have been further classed as analytic, synthetic, and identical.
q: A judgment is the mental act by which one thing is affirmed or denied of another.
The power by which we are enabled to perceive what is true or false, probable or improbable, is called by logicians the faculty of judgment.

senses.d: A calamity regarded as sent by God, by way of recompense for wrong committed; a providential punishment.
The final award; the last sentence.

Judgment.syn: Discernment; decision; determination; award; estimate; criticism; taste; discrimination; penetration; sagacity; intelligence; understanding. See Taste.
Judgment.etym: [OE. jugement, F. jugement, LL. judicamentum, fr. L. judicare. See Judge, v. i.]

senses.d: The characteristic fluid of any vegetable or animal substance; the sap or part which can be expressed from fruit, etc.; the fluid part which separates from meat in cooking.
q: An animal whose juices are unsound.
The juice of July flowers.
The juice of Egypt's grape.
Letters which Edward Digby wrote in lemon juice.
Cold water draws the juice of meat.

Juice.etym: [OE. juse, F. jus broth, gravy, juice, L. jus; akin to Skr. yūsha.]

senses.d: To moisten; to wet.
A kind of loose jacket for men.
A bodice worn instead of stays by women in the 18th century.

Jump.etym: [Cf. F. jupe a long petticoat, a skirt. Cf. Juppon.]

senses.d: To spring free from the ground by the muscular action of the feet and legs; to project one's self through the air; to spring; to bound; to leap.
q: Not the worst of the three but jumps twelve foot and a half by the square.

senses.d: To move as if by jumping; to bounce; to jolt.
q: A flock of geese jump down together.

senses.d: To coincide; to agree; to accord; to tally; — followed by with.

Jump.etym: [Akin to OD. gumpen, dial. G. gumpen, jumpen.]

senses.d: To pass by a spring or leap; to overleap; as, to jump a stream.
To cause to jump; as, he jumped his horse across the ditch.
To expose to danger; to risk; to hazard.
q: To jump a body with a dangerous physic.

senses.d: To join by a butt weld.
To bore with a jumper.
The act of jumping; a leap; a spring; a bound.
An effort; an attempt; a venture.
q: Our fortune lies Upon thisjump.

senses.d: The space traversed by a leap.
A dislocation in a stratum; a fault.
An abrupt interruption of level in a piece of brickwork or masonry.
Nice; exact; matched; fitting; precise.
Exactly; pat.
of Jump, to leap.
Any evergreen shrub or tree, of the genus Juniperus and order Coniferæ.

Juniper.etym: [L. juniperus, prop., youth-producing, and so called from its evergreen appearance, from the roots of E. juvenile, and parent. Cf. Gin the liquor.]

senses.d: The supreme deity, king of gods and men, and reputed to be the son of Saturn and Rhea; Jove. He corresponds to the Greek Zeus.

One of the planets, being the brightest except Venus, and the largest of them all, its mean diameter being about 85,000 miles. It revolves about the sun in 4,332.6 days, at a mean distance of 5.2028 from the sun, the earth's mean distance being taken as unity.

The legal power, right, or authority of a particular court to hear and determine causes, to try criminals, or to execute justice; judicial authority over a cause or class of causes; as, certain suits or actions, or the cognizance of certain crimes, are within the jurisdiction of a particular court, that is, within the limits of its authority or commission.
The authority of a sovereign power to govern or legislate; the right of making or enforcing laws; the power or right of exercising authority.
q: To live exempt From Heaven's high jurisdiction.
You wrought to be a legate; by which power You maim'd the jurisdiction of all bishops.

senses.d: Sphere of authority; the limits within which any particular power may be exercised, or within which a government or a court has authority.

Jurisdiction.etym: [L. jurisdictio; jus, juris, right, law + dictio a saying, speaking: cf. OF. jurisdiction, F. juridiction. See Just, a., and Diction.]

senses.d: Conforming or conformable to rectitude or justice; not doing wrong to any; violating no right or obligation; upright; righteous; honest; true; — said both of persons and things.
q: There is not a just man upon earth, that doeth good, and sinneth not.
Just balances, just weights, . . . shall ye have.
How should man be just with God?
We know your grace to be a man. Just and upright.

senses.d: Not transgressing the requirement of truth and propriety; conformed to the truth of things, to reason, or to a proper standard; exact; normal; reasonable; regular; due; as, a just statement; a just inference.
q: Just of thy word, in every thought sincere.
The prince is here at hand: pleaseth your lordship To meet his grace just distance 'tween our armies.
He was a comely personage, a little above just stature.
Fire fitted with just materials casts a constant heat.
When all The war shall stand ranged in its just array.
Their named alone would make a just volume.

senses.d: Rendering or disposed to render to each one his due; equitable; fair; impartial; as, just judge.
q: Men are commonly so just to virtue and goodness as to praise it in others, even when they do not practice it themselves.

Just.syn: Equitable; upright; honest; true; fair; impartial; proper; exact; normal; orderly; regular.
Just.etym: [F. juste, L. justus, fr. jus right, law, justice; orig., that which is fitting; akin to Skr. yu to join. Cf. Injury, Judge, Jury, Giusto.]

senses.d: Precisely; exactly; — in place, time, or degree; neither more nor less than is stated.
q: And having just enough, not covet more.
The god Pan guided my hand just to the heart of the beast.
To-night, at Herne's oak, just 'twixt twelve and one.

senses.d: Closely; nearly; almost.
q: Just at the point of death.

senses.d: Barely; merely; scarcely; only; by a very small space or time; as, he just missed the train; just too late.
q: A soft Etesian gale But just inspired and gently swelled the sail.

senses.d: To joust.
A joust.

The quality of being just; conformity to the principles of righteousness and rectitude in all things; strict performance of moral obligations; practical conformity to human or divine law; integrity in the dealings of men with each other; rectitude; equity; uprightness.
q: Justice and judgment are the haditation of thy throne.
The king-becoming graces, As justice, verity, temperance, stableness, . . . I have no relish of them.

senses.d: Conformity to truth and reality in expressing opinions and in conduct; fair representation of facts respecting merit or demerit; honesty; fidelity; impartiality; as, the justice of a description or of a judgment; historical justice.
The rendering to every one his due or right; just treatment; requital of desert; merited reward or punishment; that which is due to one's conduct or motives.
q: This even-handed justice Commends the ingredients of our poisoned chalice To our own lips.

senses.d: Agreeableness to right; equity; justness; as, the justice of a claim.
A person duly commissioned to hold courts, or to try and decide controversies and administer justice.

Justice.syn: Equity; law; right; rectitude; honesty; integrity; uprightness; fairness; impartiality.
Justice.etym: [F., fr. L. justitia, fr. justus just. See Just, a.]

senses.d: To administer justice to.

The act of justifying or the state of being justified; a showing or proving to be just or conformable to law, justice, right, or duty; defense; vindication; support; as, arguments in justification of the prisoner's conduct; his disobedience admits justification.
q: I hope, for my brother's justification, he wrote this but as an essay or taste of my virtue.

senses.d: The showing in court of a sufficient lawful reason why a party charged or accused did that for which he is called to answer.
The act of justifying, or the state of being justified, in respect to God's requirements.
q: Who was delivered for our offenses, and was raised again for our justification.
In such righteousness To them by faith imputed, they may find Justification toward God, and peace Of conscience.

senses.d: Adjustment of type by spacing it so as to make it exactly fill a line, or of a cut so as to hold it in the right place; also, the leads, quads, etc., used for making such adjustment.

Justification.etym: [L. justificatio: cf. F. justification. See Justify.]

senses.d: One who justifies; one who vindicates, supports, defends, or absolves.
q: Justifiers of themselves and hypocrites.
That he might be just, and the justifier of him which believeth in Jesus.

senses.d: To prove or show to be just; to vindicate; to maintain or defend as conformable to law, right, justice, propriety, or duty.
q: That to the height of this great argument I may assert eternal providence, And justify the ways of God to men.
Unless the oppression is so extreme as to justify revolution, it would not justify the evil of breaking up a government.

senses.d: To pronounce free from guilt or blame; to declare or prove to have done that which is just, right, proper, etc.; to absolve; to exonerate; to clear.
q: I can not justify whom the law condemns.

senses.d: To treat as if righteous and just; to pardon; to exculpate; to absolve.
q: By him all that believe are justified from all things, from which ye could not be justified by the law of Moses.

senses.d: To prove; to ratify; to confirm.
To make even or true, as lines of type, by proper spacing; to adjust, as type. See Justification, 4.

Justify.syn: To defend; maintain; vindicate; excuse; exculpate; absolve; exonerate.
Justify.etym: [F. justifier, L. justificare; justus just + -ficare (in comp.) to make. See Just, a., and -fy.]

senses.d: To form an even surface or true line with something else; to fit exactly.
To take oath to the ownership of property sufficient to qualify one's self as bail or surety.
To show (a person) to have had a sufficient legal reason for an act that has been made the subject of a charge or accusation.
To qualify (one's self) as a surety by taking oath to the ownership of sufficient property.
q: The production of bail in court, who there justify themselves against the exception of the plaintiff.

senses.d: To run or strike against each other; to encounter; to clash; to jostle.
q: The chariots shall rage in the streets; they shall justle one against another in the broad ways.

Justle.etym: [Freq. of joust, just, v. i. See Joust, v. i., and cf. Jostle.]

senses.d: To push; to drive; to force by running against; to jostle.
q: We justled one another out, and disputed the post for a great while.

senses.d: An encounter or shock; a jostle.
In a just manner; in conformity to law, justice, or propriety; by right; honestly; fairly; accurately.
q: Nothing can justly be despised that can not justly be blamed: where there is no choice there can be no blame.

senses.d: Jesus.
q: Jesu, give the weary Calm and sweet repose.

Jesu.etym: [L., vocative and oblique cases of Jesus.]
